title: HBM and advanced packaging
lede: The arithmetic of modern AI hardware is straightforward: a single GB200 GPU consumes more high-bandwidth memory bandwidth than a supercomputer from a decade ago, and assembling the package that delivers that bandwidth requires a small cast of specialist suppliers who do not yet appear in most investors' research universe. Serenity's cluster of ten names maps each step in that assembly chain, from compression molding to photonic inspection to wafer-level burn-in, and in most cases identifies the sole or dominant vendor at each step.
body:
## The stacking imperative

Every H100 and GB200 GPU ships with High Bandwidth Memory arranged as stacks on a substrate the size of a thumbnail. That substrate — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's (TSM) *CoWoS* (*Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate*) — has become, by one credible measure, the most constrained manufacturing resource in the global semiconductor industry. Epoch AI's supply chain research found that four companies consumed roughly 90% of global CoWoS capacity and 90% of global HBM supply in 2025, while drawing on less than 12% of advanced logic die production. The constraint was not the chips themselves. It was how they were stacked and wired together.

This observation sits at the core of a cluster Serenity assembled from late 2025 through early 2026: the chokepoints worth owning were not the headline chip designers but the narrow band of suppliers without whom the package cannot be assembled. The ten names — **TOWA** (6315.T), **MSSCorp** (6830.T), Aehr Test Systems (AEHR), SanDisk (SNDK), Micron Technology (MU), KLA Corporation (KLAC), Onto Innovation (ONTO), Applied Materials (AMAT), Lam Research (LRCX) and Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) — map almost exactly onto the bill of materials for a CoWoS HBM package.

## The specification inflection

The JEDEC HBM4 standard (JESD270-4), finalized in April 2025, doubled the per-stack memory interface from 1,024 to 2,048 bits, raising peak bandwidth from approximately 1.2 terabytes per second for HBM3E to 2 terabytes per second. The standard is not backward-compatible with HBM3E controllers, meaning every AI chip designed around NVIDIA's Vera Rubin requires a new physical-layer interface, a new interposer design and new packaging equipment. The HBM market grew from $18 billion in 2024 to $35 billion in 2025 — a 94% increase — driven almost entirely by AI training.

Micron Technology (MU) entered HBM4 mass production in Q2 calendar 2026, shipping 12-Hi stacks at pin speeds above 11 gigabits per second, ahead of the JEDEC minimum. Management confirmed that the entire calendar 2026 HBM allocation was sold under binding agreements before production began, and raised fiscal-2026 capex to $20 billion. In a structurally significant move, Micron outsourced its HBM4E base logic die to TSMC's most advanced nodes — an arrangement that ties American memory production directly to CoWoS utilization rates at Taiwan Semiconductor.

## Compression molding: the monopoly nobody talks about

TOWA (6315.T), trading at roughly ¥200 billion ($1.35 billion market cap) entering 2026, occupies an unusual competitive position. After DRAM dies are assembled via thermocompression bonding, each completed stack must be over-molded in epoxy to protect wire bonds and provide structural rigidity. TOWA claims approximately 90% of the global market for *compression molding* of HBM stacks — a share its rivals have found difficult to erode because the process requires equipment and proprietary resin formulations tuned to specific die geometries.

HBM4 introduces a precise mechanical challenge: the 2,048-bit interface requires a wider, thinner stack cross-section with less vertical clearance for encapsulant to flow into during molding. TOWA's response was *Ultra narrow gap Mold Underfill* (UMF), announced in March 2025 and positioned as the production solution for HBM4 volume assembly. The company guided FY2026 revenue to ¥71 billion ($474 million at prevailing rates), a 31% increase from the prior year, on pull from SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron's concurrent HBM3E production and HBM4 qualifications.

Serenity identified TOWA through the same monopoly-screening logic applied across their broader portfolio:

> So just putting it out there: Towa (6315), at $1.35B... Is a rare, living definition of monopoly over HBM4 (compression molding). It's been kinda flat YTD, but every memory company like $MU, SK Hynix, Samsung are their customers. And each of the memory company earnings signaled [aggressive capex].

The market was slow to respond. Despite clear upward capex signals in Micron and SK Hynix earnings, TOWA had been roughly flat through early 2026. Earnings due May 11, 2026 provided the catalyst: the stock gained over 15% in a single session on May 6, recovering toward its 52-week high. Serenity's framing was characteristically blunt elsewhere: "Names like $ONTO / $CAMT go brr. Throw in $TOWA (6315), since there's indication of aggressive memory production ramp."

## CPO inspection: MSSCorp's claimed perch

MSSCorp (6830.T), around ¥200 billion in market cap, addresses a different but adjacent chokepoint: quality control for *co-packaged optics* (CPO). CPO integrates laser transceivers directly onto the same substrate as the GPU and HBM stack — eliminating the pluggable optical module, cutting latency by roughly 10x and power consumption by roughly half for the same bandwidth. Goldman Sachs projected the total optical networking market to grow from $15 billion to $154 billion, with CPO alone contributing $91 billion of that figure. TSMC's own *COUPE* (*Compact Universal Photonic Engine*) platform, targeted for volume production in 2026, brings a photonic die onto the CoWoS substrate alongside HBM and logic — and every such die will require optical inspection to assess yield.

Serenity characterized MSSCorp as a "functional monopoly in CPO for inspection" — the verification step that determines whether CPO modules meet yield thresholds before they are assembled into expensive packages. The company stated its goal as capturing 90% of the CPO inspection market. Serenity drew an explicit distinction between materials failure analysis, an oligopoly shared with MA-tek and iST, and CPO optical inspection, the claimed single-vendor position:

> I am now long MSSCorps (6830) ~$1.4B MC. This appears to be a functional monopoly in CPO for inspection. But markets might have conflated that with Material/Failure Analysis with MA-tek and iST (oligopoly). For customers from mapping: 1. TSM 2. NVDA 3. AAPL 4. AMAT...

The research caveat is genuine. MSSCorp's primary public identity is as a materials analysis and failure analysis service provider — a close but not identical description to CPO optical inspection. If Serenity's customer-mapping exercise is correct, placing TSMC, NVIDIA and Apple as CPO inspection clients, the addressable market is substantially larger. If the distinction collapses in practice, the competitive moat is narrower than claimed.

## Aehr: testing before the expensive mistake

Aehr Test Systems (AEHR) addresses a problem that compounds with every CoWoS generation: a latent defect in a $30 silicon photonics die assembled into a $3,000 CoWoS package is a catastrophic yield event. AEHR's *FOX-XP* system performs *wafer-level burn-in* — subjecting chips to elevated voltage and temperature while still on the wafer, before dicing and packaging, precipitating early-life failures at the cheapest possible point in the manufacturing flow.

In November 2025 Aehr partnered with ISE Labs (an ASE Group subsidiary) specifically to provide *known-good-die* (KGD) screening for silicon photonics dies destined for CoWoS integration, naming CoWoS explicitly as the target package. In March 2026 a major global networking supplier ordered high-power FOX-XP systems rated at 3,500 watts per wafer for silicon photonics transceiver burn-in at hyperscale data centres.

Serenity's initial framing was deliberately speculative:

> I'm actually long $AEHR right now in the event any of the big three memory companies use them for HBM DRAM die burn in or hyperscalers expand Sonoma usage. Then there's silicon photonics, which is another area of interest. So it's more of a speculative moonshot pick to see if [they win the silicon photonics business].

The silicon photonics leg moved faster than the HBM memory leg. Quarterly bookings reached $37.2 million in Q3 FY2026, a book-to-bill above 3.5x. Serenity later described AEHR as "one of my favorite longs" with an expected inflection comparable to what they had seen in optical transceiver names. The dossier records 80% alpha above the market during the holding window — a tier-A signal in the broader reconstruction.

## SanDisk: the inference detour

SanDisk (SNDK), spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 as a pure-play NAND vehicle, is the cluster's most anomalous name. It is not an HBM company. Its stacked NAND architecture — built on BiCS *Complementary Bit-Cost Scalable* (CBA) wafer bonding — targets inference workloads where capacity (up to 512 gigabytes per stack under the proposed High Bandwidth Flash standard) matters more than the sub-nanosecond latency that HBM provides. In August 2025 SanDisk and SK Hynix signed a memorandum to jointly define the HBF specification, with first samples expected in H2 2026.

The thesis Serenity applied was more direct: SNDK was a NAND supercycle position, re-rated to semiconductor multiples following the spinoff from a hardware-manufacturer parent. They reported feeling FOMO watching the chart daily, eventually averaging into the position at around \$540 after a 7% pullback, describing it as "a possible $NVDA for me at $79B — fundamentals matter more to me than short term supply events." Gross margins expanded from the low 20s to approximately 78% in Q3 fiscal 2026 as the product mix shifted toward high-margin QLC NAND. The stock exceeded 2,400% from spinoff through spring 2026.

## The equipment layer

KLA Corporation (KLAC), Onto Innovation (ONTO), Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) are not chokepoints in the same narrow sense as TOWA. They are the machinery that builds the chokepoints. Their revenue scales directly with the pace of CoWoS and HBM capacity expansion.

KLA reported approximately $950 million in advanced packaging revenue in calendar 2025, roughly 80% above 2024, and has guided the segment to continued elevated growth. Its process control tools — covering *through-silicon via* (TSV) quality, bump coplanarity before bonding and overlay registration in CoWoS interposers — are more heavily consumed per wafer as HBM die count and package complexity increase. Management noted that HBM devices create "higher process control opportunities" because the reliability specification, not merely the yield target, demands tighter defect budgets at each stacking step.

Onto Innovation (ONTO) signed a volume purchase agreement exceeding $240 million with a leading HBM manufacturer for Dragonfly 2D inspection and 3D bump metrology systems through 2027 — the largest single packaging-specific tool contract publicly disclosed in the industry. Its Dragonfly 3Di sub-surface inspection system, capable of detecting micro-cracks from thinning and bonding at production throughput, was qualified at two major HBM customers during the period. The company guided advanced packaging revenue growth of over 30% for 2026.

Applied Materials (AMAT) occupies the broadest position in the cluster. Its Kinex *hybrid bonding* system, co-developed with Besi and launched in October 2025, is the first fully integrated die-to-wafer hybrid bonder in commercial production, placing 1,600 dies per hour with on-board metrology at bump pitches below 4 microns. Hybrid bonding replaces solder bumps with direct copper-to-copper interconnects and is the intended production technology for HBM4E. In May 2026 AMAT acquired NEXX from ASMPT for $120 million to add panel-level electrochemical deposition capability, anticipating the transition from CoWoS wafer format to 510×515mm panel format (TSMC's *CoPoS* platform) targeted for mass production around 2028.

Lam Research (LRCX) anchors the deposition side. Its SABRE 3D copper plating system revenues more than doubled in calendar 2024 on CoWoS *redistribution layer* (RDL) copper plating demand; its Aether dry photoresist was selected as production tool-of-record at a leading HBM manufacturer in January 2025, meaning each successive DRAM node refresh carries increasing Lam content per wafer. Management guided "well over $3 billion" in combined GAA-plus-advanced-packaging shipments for 2025.

Serenity identified the equipment group as downstream beneficiaries rather than lead convictions, noting: "I feel like $TSM and OSAT/advanced packaging partners are the main beneficiaries... maybe like $AMAT, $LRCX, $KLAC, $ASML and others too."

## Tower Semiconductor and the photonic layer

Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) connects the HBM cluster to the photonics architecture covered separately in this report: as the leading independent foundry for silicon photonics dies, it makes the optical engines that TSMC's COUPE platform will integrate onto CoWoS substrates alongside HBM stacks and GPU logic. Serenity's framing was succinct — "I'm long $TSEM, the $TSM of photonics" — and they took an initial position after a 21% decline in March 2026; the stock doubled in a month.

The structural logic underlying the cluster runs in a single direction: TOWA molds the HBM stack, MSSCorp inspects the photonic module, AEHR burns in the photonic dies before assembly, and Tower makes the dies that AEHR tests. Capacity constraints anywhere in that chain become yield constraints everywhere. That is, stripped of its WSB cadence, the observation Serenity has been making since late 2025 — and the reason the cluster, taken together, carries the kind of specificity that distinguishes a supply-chain thesis from a generalized bet on AI hardware spend.

concepts.definition: TSMC's advanced 2.5D packaging platform that places multiple chiplets — GPU logic, HBM memory stacks, and increasingly photonic dies — side by side on a shared silicon interposer, which is then mounted on a conventional organic substrate. CoWoS allows far shorter electrical distances between chips than a standard PCB, enabling the high bandwidth required by modern AI accelerators.

DRAM in which multiple dies are stacked vertically using through-silicon vias, then placed directly adjacent to the processor on a shared interposer. The wide parallel interface (1,024 bits per stack for HBM3E, 2,048 bits for HBM4) delivers bandwidth that far exceeds conventional DDR5, at the cost of a more complex and expensive packaging process.

An architecture that integrates optical transceivers — the devices that convert electrical signals to photons for transmission over fibre — directly onto the same package substrate as the processor, rather than in a separate pluggable module. CPO reduces latency by roughly 10x and power consumption by roughly half at equivalent bandwidth, and is considered the likely successor to pluggable optics in hyperscale AI data centres from 2026 onwards.

The manufacturing step in which a completed HBM die stack is sealed inside an epoxy compound using a press that applies the resin from above under controlled pressure and temperature, rather than injecting it from the side as in transfer molding. Compression molding is preferred for HBM because it applies lower mechanical stress to the thin stacked dies and achieves better surface flatness, which is critical for subsequent bonding to the GPU interposer.

A die that has been tested and burned-in at the wafer level before being diced and assembled into a multi-chip package. KGD screening is increasingly important as CoWoS packages become more expensive: assembling a defective die into a package worth hundreds or thousands of dollars destroys the value of all the other known-good components in that package.

A die-stacking technique that forms direct copper-to-copper electrical connections between dies without solder bumps, enabling interconnect pitches below 4 microns — roughly 10x finer than current micro-bump technology. Hybrid bonding is the roadmap path for HBM4E and beyond, promising higher bandwidth density and lower power consumption per bit transferred between the memory and logic dies.

Thin copper wiring layers deposited on an interposer or reconstituted wafer that route electrical signals between the fine-pitch bumps of a chiplet and the coarser-pitch bumps that connect to the organic substrate. In CoWoS interposers, multiple RDL layers carry high-density signal routing between GPU logic and HBM stacks; their fabrication requires precise copper plating and etch steps.

A vertical electrical connection drilled through a silicon die and filled with copper, allowing signals and power to pass between stacked dies without routing around the chip edge. TSVs are the enabling technology for HBM stacking: each DRAM die in a stack has thousands of TSVs that must be formed, inspected and precisely aligned before bonding.
